clinicalPearls: Characteristically arises posteriorly over the vocal process of the arytenoid, where the overlying mucosa is thin and closely applied to cartilage
The main drivers are laryngopharyngeal reflux, chronic throat clearing or cough, and mucosal trauma from endotracheal intubation
Presents with a globus sensation, throat discomfort or odynophonia, chronic throat clearing, and mild hoarseness
Often unilateral but may be bilateral or 'kissing' when the contralateral process is also traumatised
First-line management targets the cause with antireflux measures and voice therapy to reduce hard glottal attack and throat clearing
Surgical excision is reserved for persistent, enlarging, or airway-compromising lesions because recurrence after surgery alone is common
Malignancy is rare in this location but a lesion that fails to settle warrants biopsy to exclude neoplasia
reference.pathophysiology: A vocal fold (contact or vocal process) granuloma is an inflammatory reparative response rather than a true tumour. Mechanical trauma to the thin mucosa overlying the arytenoid vocal process, from forceful vocal contact, chronic cough or throat clearing, or an endotracheal tube, denudes the epithelium and exposes perichondrium. Acid and pepsin refluxing to the posterior larynx impair healing and perpetuate mucosal injury, so exuberant granulation tissue forms. Because the insult is ongoing, granulomas frequently recur unless the underlying reflux and phonotraumatic behaviours are corrected.
additionalDifferentials: Rheumatoid nodule or vasculitic lesion of the larynx
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to localise the lesion over the vocal process
Videostroboscopy to assess vocal fold vibration and closure
Assessment for laryngopharyngeal reflux, including symptom indices where available
Speech and language therapy voice evaluation for hard glottal attack
Biopsy of persistent or atypical lesions to exclude malignancy or specific granulomatous disease
redFlags: A lesion that continues to enlarge despite adequate antireflux and voice measures
Impaired vocal fold or arytenoid mobility
Airway compromise from a large or bilateral posterior lesion
Systemic features suggesting vasculitis, tuberculosis, or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Many granulomas resolve slowly with medical and behavioural treatment, though this can take months; recurrence is frequent if reflux and phonotrauma are not controlled, whereas long-term outcomes are good once the underlying causes are addressed.
pitfalls: Proceeding straight to excision without controlling reflux and vocal behaviour, inviting recurrence
Attributing all posterior lesions to reflux and missing an underlying malignancy or systemic disease
Failing to recognise recent intubation as a precipitating cause
Impatience with the naturally slow resolution of granulomas, prompting unnecessary surgery
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Antireflux therapy with a proton pump inhibitor and reflux-precaution lifestyle measures to allow mucosal healing
Voice therapy to reduce hard glottal attack and habitual throat clearing that perpetuate the lesion
Treat any contributing chronic cough that drives repeated mucosal trauma
Botulinum toxin injection to reduce forceful vocal-process contact in refractory cases
Reserve surgical excision for persistent, enlarging or airway-compromising lesions, or when biopsy is needed, recognising the high recurrence if the cause is uncontrolled
ENT laryngology and speech therapy referral with monitoring for recurrence
